name: Psychological trauma
statement: Psychological trauma is a clinical category rather than a judgement error, and the claim with a replication record is that talking survivors through the event prevents later disorder.
meaning: This entry is different in kind from most on this site. Trauma is not a bias. It is a diagnostic construct, and the surrounding literature is clinical rather than experimental. The page exists because a testable claim grew out of that construct and was tested hard. From the 1980s, people exposed to a shocking event were routinely offered a single structured session soon afterwards, in which they described what happened, said what they felt, and were told which reactions are normal. The intervention is called psychological debriefing, or critical incident stress debriefing in its seven-phase form. Its premise is that unprocessed traumatic material causes later disorder, and that early processing prevents it. That premise is a prediction, and randomised trials can check it. So the replication record below is about the intervention, not about whether trauma or post-traumatic stress disorder are real, which no source read here disputes.

origin.where: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, third edition
origin.note: Pai, Suris and North date the introduction of post-traumatic stress disorder as a psychiatric diagnosis to DSM-III in 1980, and write that its criteria have changed substantially at each revision since. The debriefing intervention this entry tests is younger. Stileman and Jones's reference list gives its founding description as Mitchell, J. T. (1983), 'When disaster strikes: the critical incident stress debriefing process', Journal of Emergency Medical Services 8, 36-39, which was not read for this entry.

evidence: The trials that made the reputation of debriefing were small and their results pointed the other way from the outset. Bisson, Jenkins, Alexander and Bannister randomised 133 adult burn patients to an individual or couple debriefing session or to no intervention, and 110 of them, 83%, were interviewed by an assessor blind to allocation at three and 13 months. Sixteen of the debriefed group, 26%, had PTSD at 13 months, against four of the controls, 9%. The authors note that the debriefed group started with higher questionnaire scores and more severe burns, both of which predicted worse outcome, so the comparison is not clean. Mayou, Ehlers and Hobbs followed the Oxford road-accident trial of 106 patients out to three years and reassessed 61 of them, 30 debriefed and 31 controls. Overall there was no effect of the intervention on intrusion and avoidance scores at three years, F(1,58) = 2.03, P = 0.16. Splitting by initial symptom severity changed the picture. Among patients whose baseline Impact of Event score was 24 or above, the debriefed group did worse, t(14) = 2.56, P = 0.023, observed difference 0.74 on log-transformed scores, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.28. Those high scorers went from a mean of 34.9 to 25.9 with the intervention and from 31.3 to 11.8 without it. The largest test of the seven-phase protocol is Adler and colleagues' platoon-randomised trial of 952 US peacekeepers, which reports that debriefing did not hasten recovery relative to a stress management class or to survey only, and that soldiers liked it more than the class and were not distressed by it. The trauma exposure these trials sit on is common. Kessler and colleagues, pooling 68,894 respondents across 24 countries in the WHO World Mental Health Surveys, report that 70.4% had experienced a lifetime trauma, at an average of 3.2 traumas per person.

replication.headline: Pooled across controlled studies, debriefing does not reduce later post-traumatic stress symptoms, and the separate claim that it causes harm is weaker than the claim it does nothing.
replication.detail: Three syntheses agree on the null. Rose, Bisson, Churchill and Wessely found eight trials meeting their criteria for the Cochrane review and report that single-session individual debriefing neither reduced psychological distress nor prevented PTSD onset. Their pooled odds ratio for PTSD at three to five months is 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.8. Van Emmerik, Kamphuis, Hulsbosch and Emmelkamp pooled seven studies in the Lancet and compared how much symptoms improved within each condition from before to after. Critical incident stress debriefing gave 0.13, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.55, non-CISD interventions gave 0.65, 95% CI 0.14 to 1.16, and no intervention at all gave 0.47, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.66. Their reading is that debriefing does not improve natural recovery. Stileman and Jones revisited the question in 2023 with 21 studies and 3,744 participants drawn from work-related trauma. Uncontrolled before-and-after studies produced a large apparent benefit, SMD -1.78, which they attribute to the maturational bias of that design and then exclude. What remains is a pooled SMD of -0.11, 95% CI -0.28 to 0.07, and among randomised trials alone -0.05, 95% CI -0.20 to 0.10. They report one subgroup that reaches significance, single-session debriefings at -0.19, 95% CI -0.37 to -0.02, and say it questions the standard conclusion; their own abstract still reports no consistent evidence of benefit. Whether a study followed the seven-phase protocol made no difference to the result, chi-square = 0.02, P = 0.88. The harm claim needs separating from this. It rests on the two trials above and on the Cochrane finding that at one year a single trial showed increased PTSD risk in the debriefed group, odds ratio 2.9, 95% CI 1.1 to 7.5, while the pooled figure for the two trials with follow-up just included unity, odds ratio 2.0, 95% CI 0.9 to 4.5. Stileman and Jones's long-term subgroup favours no intervention by SMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.25, which is close to nothing. Guidance moved anyway. Cochrane's stated conclusion is that compulsory debriefing of trauma victims should cease, and NICE guideline NG116 recommendation 1.6.5 reads: do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing for the prevention or treatment of PTSD.

study.cite: Stileman, H. M., & Jones, C. A. (2023). Revisiting the debriefing debate: does psychological debriefing reduce PTSD symptomology following work-related trauma? A meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology, 14, 1248924.

limits: The verdict covers one intervention, delivered soon after an event, to people who are not selected for having a disorder. It says nothing about treating established PTSD, and none of the sources read here treats it as evidence about that. It also says little about group debriefing of intact teams, which Stileman and Jones could not distinguish from individual debriefing at conventional significance, chi-square = 2.24, P = 0.13. Two results sit awkwardly against the null and are recorded rather than smoothed over. Adler and colleagues found in their peacekeeper trial that among soldiers with the highest exposure, debriefing was minimally associated with lower post-traumatic stress and aggression than the stress management class, and with more alcohol problems. Their later platoon-randomised trial of 2,297 soldiers returning from Iraq, with 1,060 followed at four months, reports that those with high combat exposure who received Battlemind debriefing had fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms, depression symptoms and sleep problems than those given stress education. Measurement is a live problem in this literature. Pai, Suris and North write that under the DSM-IV definition of witnessed exposure, research counted media reports as trauma exposure, which made almost anyone in the United States exposed to the attacks of 11 September 2001, and that DSM-5 narrowed the definition and dropped the requirement of a subjective response of fear, horror or helplessness. They also note that the DSM-5 change to the onset criterion makes new estimates hard to compare with older ones. Prevalence figures quoted from different manual editions are therefore not interchangeable. The searches behind this entry covered Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed and general web search, and were confined to debriefing, PTSD epidemiology and the diagnostic criteria. The recovered and repressed memory dispute is a separate literature with its own contested evidence and is not adjudicated here; for the experimental work on suggested and false recollection see `false-memory` and `imagination-inflation`.
misreadings: The commonest error is to read a failed intervention as a failed diagnosis. Nothing in this record says trauma or PTSD are not real, and the same surveys that supply the trial populations report substantial rates of disorder. The second error runs the other way, from 'ineffective' to 'harmful'. Two individual trials found worse outcomes in debriefed patients, and both are confounded by baseline differences that their own authors flag. The pooled estimates cluster around zero, and Cochrane's own two-trial pooled odds ratio for later PTSD includes unity. The honest summary is that the intervention did not do what it promised. The third error is to treat exposure as equivalent to disorder. Kessler and colleagues put the conditional risk of DSM-IV PTSD after a trauma at 4.0%, and it varies sharply by event type: 19.0% after rape, 11.7% after physical abuse by a romantic partner, 11.0% after being kidnapped. Most people exposed to a qualifying event do not go on to meet criteria, which is also why uncontrolled before-and-after studies of any early intervention look so good. The fourth is to assume the trials failed because practitioners did it wrong. Stileman and Jones tested that directly by comparing studies that did and did not adhere to the seven-phase model, and found no significant difference in effect between them.
